title: He Never Won Elected Office, Yet He Reshaped All of New York
dek: Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.
why: This episode is medium-density on information, but how Moses accumulated power through unelected positions, and the exact words from his 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, are valuable for understanding urban governance and how power operates.
who: Founders and investors interested in urban governance, infrastructure politics, and the mechanics of power — especially those doing government-related business or studying organizational power structures.
skip: The last ~4 minutes are listener mail about pets and gallbladder surgery, unrelated to the topic.

points.h: Never elected, yet he held enormous power
points.body: Robert Moses was never elected to any public office in his life, yet he accumulated enormous power through appointment to various government positions. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, his work includes 35 highways, 12 bridges, numerous parks, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Shea Stadium, many housing projects, two hydroelectric power plants, and the 1964 New York World's Fair. He has been dead 45 years and remains a divisive figure, and his legacy may be argued over for another century or more.

points.h: His mentor taught him not to anger voters
points.body: Moses became chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission in 1919 and learned a great deal from Belle Moskovitz. Moskovitz understood deeply how to maneuver within government to achieve goals without angering those in power. One example: in an early draft of a report, Moses recommended cutting part of the workforce, and Moskovitz reminded him that every one of those people was a voter, that they could not be angered, and that a way had to be found to cut costs without cutting so many people. This ‘don't anger the voters’ thinking ran through his later government work.

points.h: Parks were the means, highways the end
points.body: When Moses took over the parks commission, most green-space plans simply preserved natural wilderness, but he envisioned adding more manicured landscaping and dedicated recreation areas. More importantly, every time he built a new park, he made sure the project included roads connecting the park to highways — that is where the parkway came from. From the start he planned a large state park system for Long Island, all linked by new roads. In just four years in the job, he added 13 parks to Long Island, roughly 9,700 acres in total, where previously there had been only one park.

points.h: His mother lent him $20,000 to save Jones Beach
points.body: Jones Beach was originally just a sandbar on the southern edge of Long Island, almost completely submerged at high tide. Moses wanted to turn it into a great park, and most of the government and the press considered it impractical. He first used large-scale dredging to dig about 40 million cubic yards of sand from the seabed, raising the sandbar from two feet above sea level to twelve feet. But the project nearly died when the money ran out, and Moses did something highly unusual: he borrowed $20,000 from his mother, Bella, to keep the work going. He later confirmed that if his mother had not put up the money, the contractor would not have brought the equipment back to finish. Jones Beach finally opened on August 4, 1925, in a dust storm, and an estimated 1.5 million people visited in its first year.

points.h: His only campaign, and he lost badly
points.body: Moses ran for public office only once in his life. In 1934 he ran for governor of New York and was thoroughly defeated by the incumbent Democratic governor, Herbert H. Lehman. Lehman received more than 2.2 million popular votes; Moses got fewer than 1.4 million. Reporting Lehman's victory, The New York Times wrote: ‘Meanwhile, his formidable and combative opponent, Robert Moses, will be free to continue his work as the great parks commissioner.’ After this defeat he never tried to run for office again, and instead continued to expand his power through appointed positions.

points.h: 235 new playgrounds, only one in Harlem
points.body: Beginning in the 1930s, Moses greatly expanded the city's playgrounds, building 235 new ones. But a pattern began to emerge: he ignored the needs of districts with predominantly non-white populations. Of the 235 playgrounds, only one was in Harlem. In the summer of 1936 he opened 11 new swimming pools: 4 in Manhattan (including one in Harlem and one in West Harlem), 4 in Brooklyn, and 1 each in the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. The pools had new filtration and chlorination systems, heating, and underwater lighting, and were considered advanced, but they were also designed to be drained in the cooler months and used for other activities, from shuffleboard to roller skating.

points.h: ‘Tear down the slums, just build a road’
points.body: In a 1945 article in The Atlantic Monthly, Moses opened by describing how slums form: existing buildings become overcrowded, speculators add tenants, and people are packed into tenements like chickens. But the ‘cure’ he offered was this: clearing slums is in most cities accomplished indirectly — not for public, semi-public, or private housing, but for parks, playgrounds, parkways, highways, boulevards, and other public improvements. He boasted that his ‘little squad of demolition and construction devils’ had torn down more old slums than all the housing experts combined, and that ‘we built nothing but broad highways, flanked by landscaping and recreational facilities.’

points.h: Eminent domain is the only salvation
points.body: In the article Moses explicitly endorsed the use of eminent domain to acquire land. He wrote that buying large tracts of land at reasonable prices had become impossible, and that in such a situation, ‘eminent domain is the only salvation.’ Eminent domain must be exercised by the city, state, or federal government for private limited-dividend or redevelopment companies. He also criticized unions as ‘a serious obstacle to financing slum clearance,’ accusing them of insisting on retaining hourly wage rights, striking, and ‘resisting invention and improvement in the building field.’ He said this attitude was ‘unreasonable’ and would not change until a better-educated new generation of union officials appeared.

Let us have no illusions about Jones Beach as we found it. It was an isolated swampy sandbar accessible only by small boats and infrequent ferries inhabited by fishermen and loners, surf casters and assorted oddballs and beachcombers trying to get away from it all. The tales told of a lovely primitive paradise wilderness with indestructible dunes were fiction. Jones Beach was in fact a mosquito infested tidal swamp full of stagnant pools flanked by shifting dunes.

The general pattern of the development of slums is almost always the same. They begin with the overcrowding of existing buildings and the addition of tenants built by consciousness speculators to a considerable height on little land without reference to light, air, sanitation, and other standards of decent living and safety.
